Blog.article1Title: Why Spikes Lie: The Gap Between Synthetic Benchmarks and Real Blast Radius
Blog.article1Excerpt: Engineering spikes routinely surface a 5–8% quality gain in benchmarks that turns into 2–3% in production — and a 40% customer-breakage tail no one priced in. Here's how to read spike data without getting fooled.
Blog.article1Body:
Most spike reports are written for an outcome the team already wants. Synthetic benchmarks show a 5–8% quality gain, the cost numbers tilt favorably, and a public commitment quietly forms before the deeper questions land. Then the second-half spike data arrives — fine-tuning that won't transfer, infrastructure rearchitect, customer-segment breakage — and suddenly the team is choosing between a high-trust reversal and a low-trust ship. This is decision-making whiplash, and it's avoidable.

The fix isn't more spike rigor; it's reading spike data as risk data. Every spike conclusion needs three artifacts: a benchmark-vs-production delta, a blast-radius map (which customers, which services, what % of the paying base), and an explicit cascade list (the downstream risks this triggers if unresolved). When these three are produced as part of the spike — not after — the team converges on a Pxl score (probability × impact), not a yes/no recommendation. A score is comparable across the portfolio; a yes/no isn't.

Multi-agent scoring forces this discipline. Different agents pressure-test cost claims, customer impact, and infrastructure assumptions independently — surfacing the same things a careful reviewer would, but earlier and more consistently. The result isn't slower spikes. It's spikes that don't reverse, because the hidden constraints are on the table from week one. The teams who adopt this don't ship more cautiously — they ship more confidently, because the path forward is mitigated, not gambled.
Blog.article2Excerpt: Every un-modeled blast radius, un-mapped cascade, and un-recorded mitigation is risk debt — and it compounds the same way technical debt does. We measured what that costs.
Blog.article2Body:
Technical debt is a familiar villain. Risk debt is the same idea, two layers up: every change that ships without its blast radius mapped, every cascade discovered in retro instead of planning, every mitigation that lives in someone's head instead of the precedent index. Risk debt compounds because the next change inherits the previous change's un-mapped surface — and the post-mortem from the first one is the only document that captures what was learned. If nobody indexes it, the lesson disappears with the person who wrote it.

Our research across 12+ product organizations found a consistent pattern. More than 60% of risks were discovered after commit, not before. Mid-rollout reversals on un-modeled migrations cost 5–10× what the same risk would have cost in planning. And teams without a precedent retrieval discipline routinely re-litigated decisions that had been resolved a quarter earlier — because the resolution lived in a closed Slack channel, not a queryable index.

The fix isn't more rigor in the rituals. Status meetings, retros, and post-mortems all detect risk after it lands. The fix is making risk capture automatic — every Pxl score, every mitigation path, every cascade chain stored with full lineage and retrievable by similar-case search. When this is in place, risk debt stops compounding. New hires onboard against a real risk index, not tribal memory. Leadership reviews become Pxl-trend reviews, not anecdote. And the team spends less time re-discovering hidden constraints, because last quarter's spike data is now this quarter's planning input.
Blog.article3Title: Cascade Risk: Detecting the Chain Before the First Domino
Blog.article3Excerpt: A single risk is a story; the cascade chain is the plot. Most teams see the dominos one at a time. Here's how to map the chain before any of them fall.
Blog.article3Body:
When a payments outage takes down checkout, then merchant analytics, then a CRM webhook two hours later, leadership asks the same question: "why didn't we see this coming?" The honest answer is that no one was watching the chain. Each link looked stable in isolation. The risk wasn't in any one service — it was in the dependency graph that connected them, and that graph was never made explicit.

Cascade risk is the structural form of risk debt. It accumulates anywhere a change crosses a service boundary without a written-down trigger map. NEURON's approach: every Pxl-scored risk gets a cascade query. What downstream risks does this one trigger if unresolved? What past incidents share the same shape? Multi-agent reasoning walks the dependency graph from the risk outward — flagging the second-order risks that legacy review processes catch only after they fire.

This matters for two reasons. First, it changes how leaders see the portfolio: instead of a list of risks, they see a graph of risks with cascade probabilities, and their attention naturally moves to the chain heads — the small risks that would trigger several big ones. Second, it changes how teams plan mitigations. A canary rollout on a risk with three downstream cascades is not the same canary as one on a leaf-node risk; the rollback path needs to account for downstream services, not just the change site. Make the cascade explicit and the mitigation gets honest. Hide the cascade and the post-mortem writes itself.
Blog.article4Title: Mitigated-Path Engineering: Rollback-by-Default and Phased Rollouts
Blog.article4Excerpt: The verdict on a risk matters less than the path you take through it. Here's how rollback-by-default architectures and phased rollouts turn risky bets into bounded ones.
Blog.article4Body:
When risk is real, the verdict is the easy part. The hard part is the mitigated path — the operational shape of how you ship through the risk without taking the full hit if you're wrong. The teams who do this well treat every commit as a bet whose downside is bounded by an architecture, not a hope. That's mitigated-path engineering.

The first principle is rollback-by-default. If a change can't be reverted in minutes without customer impact, the change is incomplete — even if the code is shipped. This sounds extreme until you compare two outcomes: a feature flag that lets you cut a bad rollout in three minutes, vs. a permanent migration that takes three days to undo. The blast radius of the second is an order of magnitude larger, and that asymmetry should be priced into every Pxl score. NEURON's recommendation engine treats rollback paths as a first-class scoring input, not an afterthought.

The second principle is phased rollouts anchored to precedent. A 10% → 50% → 100% canary with auto-rollback at a defined error threshold is not a process; it's a contract with the data. Each phase produces evidence that either confirms or refutes the original Pxl score. If the phase data refutes it, the rollout pauses automatically — no whiplash debate, just a defined gate. This works best when paired with similar-past-case retrieval: a phased rollout shaped like one that succeeded last quarter is a known quantity, while one designed from scratch is a fresh experiment. Match the rollout to precedent and the team doesn't need to be heroic; they just need to follow the playbook the past has already written.

CognitionLayerPage.heroSubhead: Most AI tools read your data. NEURON understands it.
CognitionLayerPage.heroBody: The Cognition Layer is the architectural foundation that turns 24 disconnected tools into one coherent map of your organization. Decisions are structured records. Risks are detected by purpose-built Sentinels. Every Signal carries its evidence. Every change is auditable. Nothing is guessed.
CognitionLayerPage.s1Title: A new way of detecting what matters.
CognitionLayerPage.s1Body1: Every other AI knowledge tool follows the same shape: pipe your messages into a large language model, ask the model what's important, hope the model is right. It's slow, it hallucinates, and you can't audit why it said what it said.
CognitionLayerPage.s1Body2: NEURON inverts the pipeline. Pattern Intelligence first. Language models second. For every kind of risk worth detecting, we built a focused Sentinel — a small, fast, deterministic detector that runs cheap statistical tests against structured signals. The language model only gets involved at the end, to describe what the math already found.
CognitionLayerPage.s1Body3: The result: detection that runs in milliseconds, scales linearly, can be unit-tested, and never invents what isn't there.
CognitionLayerPage.s2Title: The six things every organization actually produces.
CognitionLayerPage.s2Intro: The Cognition Layer is built around six first-class Signal Objects. Every piece of organizational reality NEURON captures fits into one of these — typed, structured, queryable, linked.

signalObjects.name: Decision
signalObjects.captures: A choice your team made, with rationale, trade-offs, and decided-by
signalObjects.example: Switched billing provider from Stripe to Adyen — VP Finance — rationale: lower FX cost

signalObjects.name: Risk
signalObjects.captures: Something that might go wrong, with category, probability × impact, and trend
signalObjects.example: Customer onboarding pipeline at risk — schedule slippage, P×I 0.7×0.85, trending worse

signalObjects.name: Open Item
signalObjects.captures: An unresolved commitment, with urgency, owner clarity, and aging
signalObjects.example: Legal review of new ToS — unowned, soon-urgent, 17 days stale

signalObjects.name: Countermeasure
signalObjects.captures: A planned response to a risk, with assignee and due date
signalObjects.example: Add a second contractor to onboarding team — Eng Manager — due 2026-07-15

signalObjects.name: Outcome
signalObjects.captures: What actually happened after a decision or risk played out
signalObjects.example: Adyen migration completed 3 weeks ahead of plan, FX cost down 18%

signalObjects.name: Lesson Learned
signalObjects.captures: A structured takeaway from an outcome, reusable for future decisions
signalObjects.example: Vendor migrations: budget 30% buffer for double-running costs

CognitionLayerPage.s2Outro: The connective tissue: every Signal is linked to its source messages, its owning member, its project, and its history. Decisions supersede other decisions. Risks spawn Countermeasures. Outcomes produce Lessons Learned. The whole graph stays connected.
CognitionLayerPage.s3Title: Ten Sentinels. One library. Always growing.
CognitionLayerPage.s3Intro: Each Sentinel watches for one specific risk pattern. Each one is independently versioned, independently tested, and independently quality-gated. Adding a new kind of detection is a new Sentinel, not a new prompt.

sentinels.name: Unspoken Misalignment
sentinels.watches: Teams quietly drifting apart — topic divergence + graph fragmentation + engagement drop

sentinels.name: Scope Creep
sentinels.watches: Feature additions outpacing closes; backlog growth without corresponding velocity

sentinels.name: Schedule Slippage
sentinels.watches: Deliverables consistently late against original commit dates

sentinels.name: Stakeholder Disengagement
sentinels.watches: Exec or sponsor attention dropping off — fewer touches, longer response gaps

sentinels.name: Budget Overrun
sentinels.watches: Burn rate exceeding allocation, projected against cycle

sentinels.name: Quality Regression
sentinels.watches: Bug rate climbing, incident frequency rising

sentinels.name: Technical Debt Growth
sentinels.watches: Refactor backlog growing faster than new work shipping

sentinels.name: Coordination Silo
sentinels.watches: Sub-teams operating in isolation — cross-team comms below baseline

sentinels.name: Dependency Bottleneck
sentinels.watches: One team blocking many others — fan-out exceeding threshold

sentinels.name: Unresolved Blockers
sentinels.watches: Open items aging past urgency thresholds without owner action

CognitionLayerPage.s3CompoundBody: When two Sentinels correlate on the same team or project, the system names the compound pattern. Six named compound patterns ship today.
CognitionLayerPage.s4Title: If a Sentinel can't prove it works, it doesn't ship.
CognitionLayerPage.s4Body1: Every Sentinel has a Golden Dataset — a hand-labeled set of scenarios, positive and negative. The Sentinel must hit minimum precision and recall on its Golden Dataset before it merges into production. If a code change drops the numbers below the floor, CI blocks the merge.
CognitionLayerPage.s4MetricsIntro: Our keystone Sentinel — Unspoken Misalignment — currently runs at:
CognitionLayerPage.s4Metric3Note: harmonic mean of precision and recall
CognitionLayerPage.s4Outro: These aren't aspirational numbers in a deck. They're enforced in CI. Quality regression is impossible by construction.

guarantees.title: Provenance you can click into.
guarantees.body: Open any Risk in NEURON. You see the fourteen messages, in four channels, across three days, that triggered the detection. No "the AI thinks this." Just evidence.

guarantees.title: Immutable audit trail.
guarantees.body: Every change to every Signal is recorded append-only in the Provenance Chain. Enforced twice: a CI lint rule prevents code that would mutate the log, and a database trigger blocks the mutation at the storage layer. Defense in depth — the foundation for the compliance conversation you'll have with your security team.

guarantees.title: Human-approved by default.
guarantees.body: Sentinels don't write directly into the Cognition Layer. They produce Review Queue entries — pending suggestions a human approves or dismisses. Nothing in your organization's memory is there because "the AI said so." Every Signal carries the signature of a human reviewer.

CognitionLayerPage.s5Outro: For high-volume Sentinels you can configure auto-approval per-pattern. The default is human-in-the-loop. The audit trail records which Signals were human-approved and which were auto-approved — so the security team's question always has an answer.
CognitionLayerPage.s6Body1: The same person has different handles in every tool — alice@slack, alice_dev@github, Alice Chen in Monday, a.chen in your SAML directory. NEURON's Unified Identity resolves all of them into one canonical Member record, automatically, the first time any new handle appears.
CognitionLayerPage.s6Body2: Five-tier match logic: exact ID, normalized email, fuzzy name, platform-specific heuristics, and — when ambiguous — a deferred review. No manual mapping. No CSV uploads. Your org chart materializes itself.
CognitionLayerPage.s7Title: 74% fewer model tokens than a naive AI pipeline.
CognitionLayerPage.s7Body1: Because Pattern Intelligence runs first, the language model only sees the channels and time windows where structured signals actually appeared. Our multi-level extraction gate skips low-signal channels entirely — saving roughly 74% of language-model tokens on production traffic, compared to the LLM-first pipeline NEURON replaced.
CognitionLayerPage.s7Body2: Every language-model call is logged to the Provenance Chain with token count, cost, latency, and purpose. Cost is observable per workspace, per Sentinel, per call site.
CognitionLayerPage.s8Body: The Cognition Layer is implemented in PostgreSQL with pgvector for similarity search, exposed via a GraphQL API. Sentinels are versioned Python modules with YAML-configured thresholds, semver, and automatic provenance recording. Identity resolution is a 5-tier match with lazy creation of Member records. The detection pipeline runs incrementally — only the affected channels are re-evaluated when new messages land via the ingestion bridge. GraphQL subscriptions push detections to the frontend in real time. Workspace isolation is enforced at every layer — auth, query resolution, and per-workspace data filtering — so one NEURON deployment can safely host multiple organizations on shared infrastructure.
CognitionLayerPage.s9Title: Connect the first tool. Watch your organization materialize.
CognitionLayerPage.s9Intro: The moment you connect a Slack workspace, a Monday board, or a Notion database:

dayOne.title: Members appear
dayOne.body: Every person who has ever posted is recognized and de-duplicated across platforms.

dayOne.title: Decisions extract
dayOne.body: Every committed choice from the past four weeks becomes a structured Decision, with rationale and source trail.

dayOne.title: Risks surface
dayOne.body: The Sentinel Library runs against your history and proposes Risks. You triage them in the Review Queue.

dayOne.title: Open Items pile up
dayOne.body: Unresolved commitments get ranked by urgency, owner clarity, and staleness.

dayOne.title: Cross-source decisions cluster
dayOne.body: If the same decision was made in both Slack and Monday, the system detects the duplicate and merges the context.

CognitionLayerPage.s9Outro: From there the platform is reactive. New messages flow in. The Cognition Layer updates. The dashboards refresh. The Review Queue fills with new detections to triage.
CognitionLayerPage.ctaTitle: Built for organizations that need to be right.
CognitionLayerPage.ctaBody: The Cognition Layer is shipping today. Sentinels are running in production workspaces. The Provenance Chain has been audited.

rows.captures: A choice your team made, with rationale and owner.

rows.captures: A possible problem, with probability × impact and trend.
rows.example: Onboarding pipeline at risk · P×I 0.7×0.85 · trending worse

rows.captures: An unresolved commitment, with owner and age.
rows.example: Legal review of new ToS · unowned · 17 days stale

rows.captures: A planned response, with assignee and due date.
rows.example: Add second contractor · Eng Mgr · due 2026-07-15

rows.captures: What actually happened after a decision or risk played out.
rows.example: Adyen migration done 3 weeks early · FX cost down 18%

rows.captures: A reusable takeaway for future decisions.
rows.example: Vendor migrations: budget 30% buffer for double-running

signals.note: Every object links to its source, owner, and project and to the objects it caused or resolved. The graph stays connected.

DocsQuickStart.title: Quick Start
DocsQuickStart.description: This quickstart walks you through setting up Neuron and capturing your first decisions.
DocsQuickStart.createAccountP1: Go to app.neuron.unchain.com and sign up with Google or with your email and password.
DocsQuickStart.createWorkspaceP1: After signing up, you'll enter the onboarding wizard. Give your workspace a name and optionally upload a logo.
DocsQuickStart.createWorkspaceImgAlt: Workspace creation step in the onboarding wizard
DocsQuickStart.selectIndustryP1: Choose the industry that best matches your team. Neuron uses this to recommend the right AI agents for your workflow. You can also skip this step.
DocsQuickStart.chooseAgentsP1: Neuron recommends agents based on your industry. These agents analyze your team's discussions from different perspectives — identifying decisions, risks, and open items. Select the ones you want and click Continue.
DocsQuickStart.chooseAgentsTip: You can browse and add more agents by expanding the Browse more agents section.
DocsQuickStart.integrationsP1: Connect the tools your team already uses. Select the integrations you want — such as Monday.com, Jira, GitHub, or Confluence — and Neuron will walk you through connecting each one.
DocsQuickStart.integrationsP2: For each tool, Neuron provides step-by-step instructions to find your API key along with a video guide. Paste your key, click Test Connection, then Connect.
DocsQuickStart.integrationsImg2Alt: API key configuration with Test Connection
DocsQuickStart.syncDataP1: Once your integrations are verified, click Start Sync to import your data into Neuron.
DocsQuickStart.syncDataP2: When the sync completes, you'll see a confirmation screen. Click Go to Project Extraction to proceed.

DocsIntegrationChatwork.title: Chatwork
DocsIntegrationChatwork.description: Connect Chatwork to Neuron by copying your API token from the Chatwork settings page.
DocsIntegrationChatwork.overviewP1: Chatwork issues a personal API token from your Service / Packages settings page. Copy that token into Neuron's Chatwork connection screen during onboarding (or anytime from Settings → Integrations).
DocsIntegrationChatwork.step2: Go to Integrations by navigating to your Service / Packages settings page.
DocsIntegrationChatwork.step3: In the left sidebar under API, click API Token.
DocsIntegrationChatwork.step4: Your API token is displayed on this page. Click Copy to copy it.
DocsIntegrationChatwork.step5: Paste the token into Neuron's Chatwork connection screen.

DocsIntegrationGithub.title: GitHub
DocsIntegrationGithub.description: Connect GitHub to Neuron with a personal access token (classic) generated from your developer settings.
DocsIntegrationGithub.overviewP1: GitHub uses personal access tokens (classic) for third-party integrations. Generate one with the repo scope, then paste it into Neuron's GitHub connection screen.
DocsIntegrationGithub.step1: Log in to github.com and click your profile avatar in the top-right corner.
DocsIntegrationGithub.step2: Click Settings from the dropdown menu.
DocsIntegrationGithub.step3: Scroll down in the left sidebar and click Developer settings.
DocsIntegrationGithub.step4: Expand Personal access tokens and click Tokens (classic).
DocsIntegrationGithub.step5: Click Generate new token → Generate new token (classic).
DocsIntegrationGithub.step6: Enter a Note (e.g., "Neuron") to label the token, and set an Expiration period (90 days recommended).
DocsIntegrationGithub.step7: Select the scopes Neuron needs (at minimum, check repo for repository access).
DocsIntegrationGithub.step8: Scroll down and click Generate token.
DocsIntegrationGithub.step9: Copy the token immediately — GitHub will only show it once.
DocsIntegrationGithub.step10: Paste the token into Neuron's GitHub connection screen.

DocsIntegrationDiscord.title: Discord
DocsIntegrationDiscord.description: Create a Discord application and connect it to Neuron with the Application ID, Public Key, and Bot Token.
DocsIntegrationDiscord.overviewP1: Discord integrations are built on top of a Developer Portal application. Create one for Neuron, then copy its Application ID, Public Key, and Bot Token into Neuron's Discord connection screen.
DocsIntegrationDiscord.step1: Go to the Discord Developer Portal and log in.
DocsIntegrationDiscord.step2: Click New Application in the top-right corner.
DocsIntegrationDiscord.step3: Enter a Name for the app (e.g., "Neuron") and click Create.
DocsIntegrationDiscord.step4: On the General Information page, you'll see your Application ID and Public Key. Copy both using the Copy buttons.
DocsIntegrationDiscord.step5: In the left sidebar, click Bot.
DocsIntegrationDiscord.step6: Click Reset Token and verify your identity (Discord may prompt for your password or MFA).
DocsIntegrationDiscord.step7: Your new bot token will be displayed. Click Copy to copy it — you won't be able to see it again.
DocsIntegrationDiscord.step8: Paste the Application ID, Public Key, and Bot Token into Neuron's Discord connection screen.

DocsIntegrationGranola.title: Granola
DocsIntegrationGranola.description: Generate a Granola API key from the desktop app's Connectors settings and paste it into Neuron.
DocsIntegrationGranola.overviewP1: Granola exposes API keys from its desktop app's Settings panel. Generate a Personal API key (or Enterprise for admins) and paste it into Neuron's Granola connection screen.
DocsIntegrationGranola.step1: Open the Granola desktop app and go to Settings.
DocsIntegrationGranola.step2: In the left sidebar under Connectors, click API.
DocsIntegrationGranola.step4: In the "Generate API Key" dialog, select Personal API (accesses notes you own and notes shared with you) or Enterprise API (for enterprise admins only).
DocsIntegrationGranola.step5: Click Generate and wait for the key to be created.
DocsIntegrationGranola.step6: Copy the API key and paste it into Neuron's Granola connection screen.

DocsIntegrationHubspot.title: HubSpot
DocsIntegrationHubspot.description: Connect HubSpot to Neuron by generating a personal access key from your developer settings.
DocsIntegrationHubspot.overviewP1: HubSpot uses personal access keys for programmatic integrations. Generate one from Development → Keys, select the scopes Neuron needs, then paste the key into Neuron's HubSpot connection screen.
DocsIntegrationHubspot.step2: Click the Settings gear icon in the bottom-left of the sidebar.
DocsIntegrationHubspot.step3: In the left sidebar, navigate to Development (under the developer overview at app.hubspot.com/developer-overview).
DocsIntegrationHubspot.step4: Expand Keys in the left sidebar and click Personal Access Key.
DocsIntegrationHubspot.step5: Select the scopes / permissions you want the key to have, then click Generate personal access key.
DocsIntegrationHubspot.step6: Once generated, click Show or Copy to copy your Personal Access Key.
DocsIntegrationHubspot.step7: Paste the key into Neuron's HubSpot connection screen.

DocsIntegrationJira.title: Jira
DocsIntegrationJira.description: Connect Jira to Neuron by creating an API token in your Atlassian account security settings.
DocsIntegrationJira.overviewP1: Jira (and the rest of Atlassian Cloud) uses account-wide API tokens. Create one from id.atlassian.com, copy it immediately, and paste it into Neuron's Jira connection screen.
DocsIntegrationJira.step1: Go to your Atlassian Account settings at id.atlassian.com.
DocsIntegrationJira.step2: Click Security in the top navigation bar.
DocsIntegrationJira.step3: Navigate to the API Tokens section (at id.atlassian.com/manage-profile/security/api-tokens).
DocsIntegrationJira.step5: Enter a Name for the token (e.g., "Neuron") and set an Expiration date.
DocsIntegrationJira.step7: Copy the token immediately — you won't be able to see it again after closing this dialog.
DocsIntegrationJira.step8: Paste the token into Neuron's Jira connection screen.

DocsIntegrationKintone.title: Kintone
DocsIntegrationKintone.description: Generate a Kintone API token from the Users & system administration page and paste it into Neuron.
DocsIntegrationKintone.overviewP1: Kintone issues API tokens scoped to read or write apps. Generate one with read scope from your portal's admin page, then paste it into Neuron's Kintone connection screen.
DocsIntegrationKintone.step1: Log in to your Kintone portal (e.g., yourcompany.kintone.com).
DocsIntegrationKintone.step2: Click your profile name in the top-right corner and select Users & system administration.
DocsIntegrationKintone.step3: In the left sidebar under Integrations, click API tokens.
DocsIntegrationKintone.step5: Enter an Overview description (e.g., "Neuron"), select a Scope (Read is sufficient), and set a Validity period.
DocsIntegrationKintone.step7: Copy the API token immediately — you won't be able to view it again after leaving the page.
DocsIntegrationKintone.step8: Paste the token into Neuron's Kintone connection screen.

DocsIntegrationLinear.title: Linear
DocsIntegrationLinear.description: Connect Linear to Neuron with a personal API key from your Security & access settings.
DocsIntegrationLinear.overviewP1: Linear uses personal API keys for third-party integrations. Generate one from Settings → Security & access and paste it into Neuron's Linear connection screen before leaving the page (Linear only shows the key once).
DocsIntegrationLinear.step3: Scroll down to the Personal API keys section.
DocsIntegrationLinear.step6: Copy the API key immediately — Linear will not show it again after you leave the page.
DocsIntegrationLinear.step7: Paste the key into Neuron's Linear connection screen.

DocsIntegrationMonday.title: Monday.com
DocsIntegrationMonday.description: Connect Monday.com to Neuron by copying your personal API token from the Administration panel.
DocsIntegrationMonday.overviewP1: Monday.com exposes a per-user Personal API token from the Administration panel. Copy it into Neuron's Monday.com connection screen.
DocsIntegrationMonday.step2: Click your profile avatar in the top-right corner and go to Administration.
DocsIntegrationMonday.step3: In the left sidebar, expand Connections and click Personal API token.
DocsIntegrationMonday.step4: Your Personal API Token is displayed on this page. Click Copy to copy it.
DocsIntegrationMonday.step5: Paste the token into Neuron's Monday.com connection screen.

DocsIntegrationNotion.title: Notion
DocsIntegrationNotion.description: Create a Notion internal integration and paste its secret into Neuron.
DocsIntegrationNotion.overviewP1: Notion connects via internal integrations scoped to one workspace. Create one for Neuron, copy the integration secret, and paste it into Neuron's Notion connection screen.
DocsIntegrationNotion.step1: Go to notion.so/profile and log in.
DocsIntegrationNotion.step2: In the left sidebar under Build, click Internal integrations.
DocsIntegrationNotion.step4: Enter an Integration name (e.g., "Neuron"), select the Associated workspace you want Neuron to access, and click Create.
DocsIntegrationNotion.step5: On the integration page, you'll see the Internal integration secret (hidden by default). Click Show to reveal it, then copy the secret.
DocsIntegrationNotion.step6: Paste the secret into Neuron's Notion connection screen.

DocsIntegrationRecallai.title: Recall.ai
DocsIntegrationRecallai.description: Generate a Recall.ai API key from your dashboard's Developers section and paste it into Neuron.
DocsIntegrationRecallai.overviewP1: Recall.ai issues API keys from your dashboard's Developers section. Generate one, copy it, and paste it into Neuron's Recall connection screen.
DocsIntegrationRecallai.step1: Log in to your Recall.ai dashboard (e.g., ap-northeast-1.recall.ai/dashboard).
DocsIntegrationRecallai.step2: In the left sidebar under Account, click Developers.
DocsIntegrationRecallai.step3: On the API Keys & Secrets tab, click + New API Key.
DocsIntegrationRecallai.step4: Enter a Name for the key (e.g., "Neuron") and click Create Key.
DocsIntegrationRecallai.step6: Paste the key into Neuron's Recall connection screen.

DocsIntegrationSlack.title: Slack
DocsIntegrationSlack.description: Create a Slack app, generate an app-level token, and paste it into Neuron's Slack connection screen.
DocsIntegrationSlack.overviewP1: Slack integrations are built on top of Slack apps. Create one from api.slack.com/apps, generate an app-level token (starts with xapp-), and paste it into Neuron's Slack connection screen along with the values from the Basic Information page.
DocsIntegrationSlack.step1: Go to api.slack.com/apps and sign in.
DocsIntegrationSlack.step2: Click Create an App, choose From scratch, enter an app name (e.g., "Neuron"), select your workspace, and complete the creation wizard.
DocsIntegrationSlack.step3: After creation, you'll land on the app's Basic Information page. Here you can find your App ID, Client ID, Client Secret, and Signing Secret.
DocsIntegrationSlack.step4: Scroll down to the App-Level Tokens section and click Generate Token.
DocsIntegrationSlack.step5: Enter a Token Name (e.g., "Neuron"), add the required scopes, and click Generate.
DocsIntegrationSlack.step6: Copy the generated token (starts with xapp-).
DocsIntegrationSlack.step7: Paste the token into Neuron's Slack connection screen.
